name: Chairtax
what: At the interval you set, Chairtax covers your Mac's screen and gives it back once the camera has counted your reps: squats, or one of five other movements.
glance: Squats, chair stands, jumping jacks, high knees, overhead reach and side bends
Cub, Brown bear and Grizzly, from a card you can dismiss to a screen that stays covered
Reps are counted on the Mac; the picture is never saved, uploaded or shown
macOS 14 or later, from chairtax.app or the Mac App Store
archHi:
Chairtax is a Mac menu-bar app that takes the screen at the interval you set and gives it back when the camera has counted your reps. Setup picks the movement, the reps per break, the workday and the rank; after that, breaks run through the day on their own.

  1. Heads up. Thirty seconds before a break, a notice gives the movement and the target. If another app is using the camera or microphone, as on a video call, the break waits five minutes and checks again.
  2. Get moving. The screen is covered on every display. You stand where the camera can see you and do the reps, while a stick figure on the break screen follows your movement and the count climbs.
  3. Back to work. At the target the screen comes back, and the break goes on your record: the streak, the reps in total, the last 14 days and the award shields.

The rank decides how hard a break is to skip. Cub puts a card over your work that you can dismiss, Brown bear covers the screen and allows a few skips a day, and Grizzly keeps it covered until the reps are done. Every rank has Emergency override, which gives the screen back after 60 seconds, and every break ends on its own after 15 minutes.

Because the counting happens on the Mac, the camera picture never leaves it. The download's one network call is its licence check, and the Mac App Store build makes none.
arch:
Three Swift layers: ChairtaxCore holds every decision as plain logic with no AppKit, ChairtaxShield owns the windows that cover the screen, and the app wires the camera, Vision, the scheduler, the menu bar and the break screen around them.

  • A break is one state machine. Idle, notice, warming, shielded, detecting, counting, overriding and ended. Camera frames, a held framing, each rep, the override button and a tick about once a second go in; effects such as open the camera, save the break and raise the shield come out. Every timer reads monotonic uptime, so moving the Mac's clock cannot shorten a break.
  • Calls are found at the device level. Before a break, every camera is checked through CoreMediaIO and the default microphone through Core Audio for use by another process; AVFoundation's in-use flag never reported a call in the measurements made before the build. A device in use postpones the break five minutes, and five minutes without keyboard or mouse input reschedules it.
  • Saved before the screen is taken. The active break is written to a temporary file, fsynced and renamed into place before the shield goes up, and written again on every counted rep. A force-quit or crash resumes the break with its reps and its original 15-minute ceiling. Finished breaks go to an append-only log, one fsynced JSON line each.
  • A watchdog gives the screen back. It runs on its own thread, away from the main run loop, and ends the process if the shield is still up 20 minutes after it rose, so a hung main thread cannot hold the screen.

Each rank is a window level and a set of macOS presentation options:

RankThe breakmacOS options while it is up
Cuba translucent card over your work, which can be dismissednone
Brown bearevery display covered at the shielding window level, with a few skips a dayDock and menu bar hidden
Grizzlyevery display covered until the reps are done, with no skipsDock and menu bar hidden and app switching off; the download also turns off Force Quit, Log Out and the Apple menu, which the App Store build leaves working
  • Vision reads every frame on the Mac. Each frame runs Apple Vision's 2D body-pose request, with the face and upper-body rectangle requests in the same call where the movement reads them. Where the user's shoulders do not read, as at close range, a second pose pass runs on the frame shrunk to 0.4 inside a black frame, which gives a body at the lens room to be found. It feeds the stick figure and the close-range knee and jumping-jack counts.
  • A frame budget protects the frame rate. The stick figure's second pass runs only while the median times of both passes stay within 40 ms together, a 25 frames-a-second floor; the camera discards late frames, so a slow Mac loses frames and never stalls.
  • One person is followed. A person lock tracks every body in view from frame to frame, matched on position, velocity and size. The break follows the largest, most central readable body, never a body that was in view at the same time as the user, and follows someone new only after the user has been out of sight for five seconds. A mirror's reflection, a poster or a second person in the room cannot take over the count.
  • Each movement is a definition. One table gives each movement its signal (the shoulder line, depth, lean, arms or knees), its thresholds, its rule for a held framing and its status-line behaviour. Squat depth is read from the shoulders, the neck or the face, so a squat counts at 0.5 to 1.0 m, where the shoulders drop out of the frame.
  • The energy estimate is a published method. Setup turns age, sex, weight and the schedule into the energy the breaks use each week and year, using the Compendium of Physical Activities' corrected-MET method with Schofield resting rates, net of sitting.
  • Licence keys are signed and held to one Mac. Paddle's completed-checkout webhook reaches a Cloudflare Worker, which checks Paddle's HMAC signature and mints an Ed25519-signed key. The app activates with the key and a SHA-256 hash of the Mac's hardware UUID, so the raw UUID never leaves the Mac, and receives a signed token good for 60 days that it renews in the last 30.
  • The challenge is read from the app's own record. The money-back challenge asks for 100 camera-counted reps on 16 of the first 30 days. Its claim code carries the daily counts, a running SHA-256 chain over the record's lines that changes if any line is edited, dropped or reordered, and a count of wall-clock jumps measured against uptime.
proc:
• A Swift package, a Worker and a static site. Native Swift on macOS 14 and later, with no Xcode project: a SwiftPM package of three targets, AppKit for the windows that cover the screen and SwiftUI for the break screen, setup and Settings, and a script that assembles the .app. Camera frames come through AVFoundation and are read by Apple Vision. Licences run on a Cloudflare Worker with KV storage and Paddle checkout; chairtax.app is static pages on Cloudflare Pages, with its copy managed in stet.
  • Functional core, imperative shell. The break state machine, rep counters, calibration, person lock, records, awards, challenge and licence check live in ChairtaxCore as plain code over time and pose samples passed in. The camera, the windows, the disk and the network stay at the edges.
  • A reducer with effects as data. The break machine never acts on the world itself. It returns effects, and the session performs them in order, which is how saving the break is guaranteed to finish before the shield is raised.
  • Write-ahead state and an append-only log. The active break is on disk before the shield goes up, and the break history is only ever appended to. A line that fails to decode is skipped, so one bad line never costs the whole history.
  • A dead-man's switch. The watchdog holds a deadline on its own thread and exits the process when it passes, independent of anything the main thread is doing.
  • One source tree, two builds. The download and the Mac App Store build compile from the same code, with compile-time flags marking the differences: the App Store build is sandboxed and carries no licence, checkout or money-back code. A release script refuses any binary that still carries a developer switch, or, for the App Store build, the download's money copy.
  • Feature flags for the counters. Each change to how a movement is counted ships behind a named candidate. A release build runs the shipped set, and a debug build can run any other set by name.
  • Record and replay. A debug build records a break's raw Vision output, rounded exactly as the live path rounds it, so a recording rebuilds every pose sample bit for bit. A separate tool, chairtax-replay, runs recordings back through the same core code, so each counting change is measured against real sessions before it ships.
  • Idempotent licence minting. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the webhook and the thanks page's fallback mint the same key for the same transaction, and a redelivered webhook changes nothing.
  • Privacy as a build rule. The camera is the only permission the app requests, and the app sends no analytics. The download makes one kind of network call, the licence check, and the App Store build makes none.
